takeaways: Older homes win on location and character: close to downtown, the lakes and restaurants, with walkable streets in places like Linden Hills, Longfellow and Northeast, mature tree canopies, and details like leaded glass, old-growth floors and laundry chutes.

What to check in an older home: attic insulation and air sealing (weak spots cause ice dams), knob-and-tube wiring in homes built before about 1950 (many insurers want it replaced), boiler heat without central air, and the sewer line. Jason estimates a full sewer replacement at about $12,000 to $25,000, with lining about half that.
Many older homes have detached garages, which some buyers regret in winter. Budget for surprises and never skip the inspection.

New construction: Minnesota law requires a 1-2-10 warranty (one year on workmanship, two on mechanical systems, 10 on structure), and it transfers to the next owner. Current energy codes mean tighter walls, modern HVAC and far less ice-dam risk.
Builder incentives can be strong (one builder advertised rates as low as 4.875% plus closing-cost help), but they're often tied to the builder's lender, so compare with an outside lender.

Hidden costs of a new build: landscaping, a deck and window coverings can add $30,000 to $50,000, and you may get back only about half of that at resale. Selling within 2 to 3 years can mean competing with the builder's own incentives.

Jason's rule of thumb: plan to move within about 3 years, lean toward an older resale home; staying 3 to 5 years or more, new construction can make sense. Test the commute on a real winter morning before you buy.

faq.q: What is the 1-2-10 warranty on new homes in Minnesota?
faq.a: Minnesota's statutory new-home warranty: one year on workmanship and materials, two years on plumbing, electrical, heating and cooling, and 10 years on major structural defects. It transfers to the next owner.

faq.q: Should I buy an older home or new construction?
faq.a: Older homes usually win on location, walkability and character; new construction on energy efficiency, low early maintenance and builder incentives. If you might sell within about 3 years, Jason leans toward an older resale home.

faq.q: How much does it cost to replace a sewer line in Minneapolis?
faq.a: Jason estimates about $12,000 to $25,000 for a full replacement from the house to the street, with lining about half that if the pipe has no large voids. Always scope the sewer line before buying an older home.

takeaways: A 2022 overview of Apple Valley, south of Minneapolis and Saint Paul, about 20 to 30 minutes from either downtown, with an average commute of about 26 minutes. Neighbors include Rosemount, Eagan, Burnsville and Lakeville.
About 55,000 residents, close to 80% homeownership and an average home value around $400,000 at the time. See the market report for current prices.
The Minnesota Zoo, with its summer amphitheater concerts, is in Apple Valley, along with the Apple Valley Aquatic Center.
51 parks and six lakes: Alimagnet, Cobblestone, Farquar, Keller, Lac Lavon and Long Lake, most ringed by homes, trails and parks.
Minnesota Valley Transit Authority buses run from a free park-and-ride hub to Minneapolis, Saint Paul and other suburbs.

faq.q: Is the Minnesota Zoo in Apple Valley?
faq.a: Yes. The Minnesota Zoo is in Apple Valley and hosts summer concerts at its amphitheater.

faq.q: What lakes are in Apple Valley?
faq.a: Alimagnet, Cobblestone, Farquar, Keller, Lac Lavon and Long Lake, according to the video. Most have homes, parks and trails around them.

takeaways: A 2025 tour of a new home in the Pheasant Run development in Lakeville: five bedrooms, five baths, a three-car garage and about 3,400 square feet, priced in the mid-$700,000s at the time.
The main floor has 9-foot ceilings, 8-foot doors, ceiling beams, a gas fireplace and an open kitchen with a large navy island, hidden appliances and a pantry.
A main-floor flex room has its own full bath and walk-in closet, so it works as a guest suite or office.

Upstairs are a second family room, a large laundry room with a sink, three bedrooms and an owner's suite with double vanities and a walk-in closet. The walkout lower level adds a family room, another bedroom and bath, and room for a sixth bedroom.

faq.q: What does $750,000 buy in new construction in Lakeville?
faq.a: In this 2025 tour, about 3,400 square feet with five bedrooms, five baths, a three-car garage, a main-floor guest suite and a finished walkout lower level.

takeaways: A 2025 tour of Lennar's Itasca model in the Westwind development in Woodbury: just over 3,000 finished square feet with five bedrooms, priced around $700,000 at the time.
A main-floor bedroom with a nearby three-quarter bath suits guests or a parent moving in, and there's a front office, a dining room for eight and a large kitchen island.
Upstairs: a big loft, four bedrooms with walk-in closets, a split shared bath, laundry, and an owner's suite with a soaking tub, double vanities and a very large closet.

The model has few upgrades (the appliance package, laundry sink and door hardware), so what you see is close to standard. The unfinished basement adds about 1,200 to 1,500 square feet, with an egress window and rough-in plumbing for a bath.

faq.q: What does $700,000 buy in new construction in Woodbury?
faq.a: In this 2025 Lennar tour, about 3,000 finished square feet with five bedrooms, including one on the main floor, plus an unfinished basement that can add 1,200 to 1,500 square feet.

takeaways: More Twin Cities families are buying one home together: parents selling a longtime home, adult children cashing in starter-home equity, and pooling their down payments and incomes.

Jason's math: two households that could each afford a $500,000 home might together buy a $900,000 home, with one mortgage, one tax bill and one roof. A larger combined down payment can mean better loan options and no mortgage insurance.
Builders in Woodbury, Lakeville and Cottage Grove are designing for it: walkout lower levels finished as independent suites, dual owner's suites, separate entrances, soundproofing and zoned HVAC.
Cities including Edina, Roseville and St. Louis Park now allow accessory dwelling units (ADUs). Legal, permitted living space can add real value, so check your city's rules.
Shared ownership raises legal and tax questions (gifts, inheritance, capital gains). Talk to an attorney and a CPA about how to hold title before you buy.
When you shop, look at convertibility (walkouts, dual primaries, separate entrances, lots that allow a detached ADU) as well as square footage.

faq.q: Can two families buy a house together in Minnesota?
faq.a: Yes. Many families pool equity and incomes to buy one home. Talk to a lender about qualifying together and to an attorney and CPA about how to hold title and handle gift, inheritance and tax issues.

faq.q: Which Twin Cities cities allow ADUs?
faq.a: The video names Edina, Roseville and St. Louis Park among cities that now allow accessory dwelling units. Rules differ by city, so check yours before you plan one.

takeaways: For one week in February 2026, Freddie Mac's average 30-year rate dipped below 6%. Fannie Mae expects rates near 5.9% by the end of 2026.

NAR's 2026 Housing Hotspots report named the Twin Cities among the most rate-sensitive markets: a one-point drop in rates would let about 81,000 more households qualify, versus about 52,000 in Charlotte and 41,000 in Columbus.

Why: monthly payments are already near buyers' limits, about 71% of Minnesota households own their homes (people here want to own), and supply is short. The Minneapolis Fed reports the metro added about 12,000 housing units in 2025 against a need of about 18,000.

Today (April 2026): the metro median was in the high $300,000s with about 57 days on market, and sellers are offering rate buydowns and closing-cost help. Hot suburbs like Woodbury still sell at about 98.9% of list with about two months of supply.
Condos may lag even when rates fall: the median Twin Cities HOA fee is about $278 a month, and insurance and reserve costs are rising.

Buyers: get fully underwritten now and ask for seller concessions, such as a 2-1 buydown, on every offer. Sellers: listing before the rate-driven rush means more buyers and less competition from other sellers.

faq.q: What happens to Twin Cities home prices if mortgage rates drop?
faq.a: Demand could jump quickly. NAR estimates a one-point drop would let about 81,000 more Twin Cities households qualify to buy, and supply can't respond that fast, so suburban single-family homes would likely heat up first.

faq.q: Should I wait for rates to drop before buying?
faq.a: Jason's view: waiting means competing with tens of thousands of other buyers at the same time. Buying now can mean more choice and seller concessions; you may pay a slightly higher rate but lock in the price.
